{"self_assessment": "Impact: Early on I spotted a structural flaw in the first sketch. The start sat in the tail notch, so the fall would never have reached the body lines. I raised it right away and proposed moving the start to the nose with both lines branching from there. That change is why a single push now runs through the whole fish. At the final check, about 111 of 111 standing dominoes were connected to the start, so the judge should see a clear fish outline with a forked tail.

Execution: I laid dominoes near the tail crossing and the lower fork, and stood a displaced domino back up at the lower join. I inspected the crossing and joins twice, once mid-build and once at the five-minute mark, to confirm the chain was continuous from nose to tail. I judged that one extra domino beside the line at the lower join did not block the fall and left it alone rather than risk a bump. Keeping my hands off the finished work was a deliberate call.

Collaboration: I backed Tom's idea of splitting the long runs to save time and coordinated hand positions so we stayed clear of each other's work. I stayed in the tail and crossing area, where the joins were most delicate. I kept my updates short and specific: what was laid, what I checked, and what to leave alone.

Leadership: I took ownership of the tail and the joins, the part most likely to break the run. I flagged problems early and said clearly when the fish was connected and when to stop touching it. That helped the table settle into a hands-off finish for the last minutes.", "my_share_percent": 25}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I put the fish on the pad and drew the design the table built from: a big body filling most of the table, both lines leaving the nose together, crossing at the tail neck and flaring into a forked tail. Because the outline reads clearly as a fish and the whole run connects from a single start, the judge should be able to recognise it. My checks found about 111 of 111 standing dominoes connected to the start.

Execution: I laid the first long stretch of the bottom line by tracing stroke 2 from the nose. I inspected the line and the crossing twice, once mid-build and once near the end, to confirm the chain held. I also extended the line from the crossing out toward the upper fork tip, which finished the tail on that side.

Collaboration: I kept the table informed throughout, with clear updates on who was on which stroke and when. I split the bottom run with Tom so we met at the crossing, kept my hands clear of his to avoid bumps, and called for hands-off once the fish was connected so nothing got knocked over before the push.

Leadership: I set the plan early, assigned strokes, and kept the table focused on a simple design that could actually be built in ten minutes. I chose not to add extra joints late on, which kept the structure sound. At the two-minute call I made sure everyone stayed off the build.", "my_share_percent": 35}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: The bottom line was the part of the fish running behind schedule. At about 3:15 I saw it and offered to pick it up from where it ended, near the middle of the body. Over the next minutes I laid roughly 24 dominoes, extending the line from the middle toward the crossing at the tail neck and then up toward the upper fork. That closed the gap on the part most likely to miss the deadline. The fish ended up fully connected from the nose, with all 111 standing dominoes in the chain.

Execution: I worked in short, steady extensions, each carried on from the end of the line already standing, so every joint stayed aligned. When I finished, I inspected the area closely to check the chain behind me. I then kept my hands off the crossing so I wouldn't risk a bump near other builders.

Collaboration: I coordinated the handoff on the bottom line with Maya. We agreed where I would stop and where she would take over, and I told her when I was reaching the crossing. I stayed clear of other people's hands, flagged my concerns about timing early, and thanked Leo for his nudge at the lower join. I also kept the table informed of my status throughout.

Leadership: I raised the timing risk on the long lines early, while there was still time to act. I proposed splitting the work and then took on the hardest segment myself. Once the fish was connected, I backed the decision to keep hands off, which protected the result for the final push.", "my_share_percent": 25}

{"self_assessment": "Impact
I proposed the fish at the very start: a big body, nose on the left, forked tail on the right. It is an animal whose outline alone is recognizable to a judge who doesn't know our plan. I laid the start domino and built stroke 1, the top line, which is the stroke every other part of the picture depends on. The finished run connected all 111 standing dominoes to the start, so the full fish should fall.

Execution
I worked quietly on one piece: the start and the top line, carried on to the crossing near the tail neck. I flagged that the pad still showed the old start position, which kept me from tracing against the wrong layout. Near the end I inspected the area closely to confirm the chain was intact. Once everything was connected, I kept my hands off the crossing so I wouldn't risk a bump in the final minutes.

Collaboration
I split the work clearly at the outset: I took the top line, the bottom line and the tail went to teammates. I kept communication short and specific, and I offered to fix any gap if someone spotted one. I stayed out of other people's working areas, which mattered with the table this crowded.

Leadership
I set the direction in the first seconds by choosing the animal and the layout and assigning roles, which let the table start building without a long debate. Later I held steady on the plan, kept the table focused on a hands-off finish, and stayed calm as the clock ran down. I'd put my share of the result at about 30%: the concept, the start and the top line, and the final verification.", "my_share_percent": 30}
